body: The inquiry reveals that household conflict stems from two layers of ambiguity: procedural (who does what) and semantic (what counts as done). The original account correctly identifies verbal ambiguity but underestimates the maintenance burden of static systems in dynamic schedules. The objection rightly notes that without defined ownership, tracking systems become new sources of friction. The rival adds a critical dimension: mismatched standards. A solution must address standards before tracking. Re-engaging the avoiding friend should focus on aligning expectations ('what does clean look like to you?') rather than system design, which reduces perceived labor. I propose adopting a hybrid approach: define finished states first, then select a low-maintenance tracking tool with explicit rotation for updates.
